t: #4013 Count Subarrays With Even Odd Ratio II — Editorial
o: A subarray is valid when its even count x and odd count y satisfy y > 0 and x/y ≤ a/b, i.e. b·x − a·y ≤ 0. Using prefix counts E and O of evens and odds, the subarray (i, j] has x = E_j − E_i, y = O_j − O_i, so the condition becomes b·E_j − a·O_j ≤ b·E_i − a·O_i. Define f(k) = b·E_k − a·O_k; we must count pairs i < j with f(i) ≤ f(j) — a classic 'count non-inversions' problem solvable with merge sort or a BIT. Note y = 0 (all-even subarray) automatically fails since then b·x > 0, so no special casing is needed. Products reach 10⁹ · 10⁵ = 10¹⁴, requiring 64-bit integers.
k: Rewrite x/y ≤ a/b exactly as b·x − a·y ≤ 0 to avoid floating point.
With prefix counts this becomes: count pairs i < j with f(i) ≤ f(j), where f(k) = b·E_k − a·O_k.
All-even subarrays fail automatically, so the y > 0 requirement needs no extra work.
Values reach ~10¹⁴, so use 64-bit arithmetic everywhere.

a.i: Compute the prefix array f, then for every pair (i, j) with i < j check f(i) ≤ f(j) directly. Simple and correct; too slow only for the largest inputs, but a great baseline to validate the fast solution.
s: Build f[k] = b·(#evens in prefix k) − a·(#odds in prefix k), including the empty prefix f[0] = 0.
Double loop over all pairs i < j.
a.t: O(n²) — all pairs of prefix indices.

a.n: Approach 2: Divide and Conquer (Merge Sort) Counting — Optimal
a.i: During merge sort of f, whenever we take an element from the left half, every remaining element in the right half is ≥ it (both halves sorted), contributing len(rightRemaining) valid pairs. Summing these contributions counts exactly the pairs i < j with f(i) ≤ f(j) in O(n log n).
s: Recursively split f, sorting halves and accumulating cross-pair counts.
In the merge step, when l[i] ≤ r[j], add (len(r) − j) to the count and advance i.
a.t: O(n log n) — standard merge sort recursion with O(1) amortized pair accounting per merge step.

w: Lead with the algebraic reduction (ratio comparison → linear inequality on prefixes), then present merge-sort counting; a BIT over compressed f-values works identically if you prefer Fenwick trees. Pitfalls: comparing ratios with floating point (precision bugs), 32-bit overflow of b·E, and forgetting the empty prefix f[0] = 0 (subarrays starting at index 0). Edge cases: all-even arrays return 0 (Example 3); a/b ≥ huge ratios make everything with y > 0 valid. Follow-ups: count subarrays with strict inequality (just change ≤ to < in the merge), or handle streaming queries with an online BIT.
